props.title: A data harness in one breath
items: The model is the engine; the harness is the car
Prepare data before the question: rows for numbers, chunks for prose
One facts table: value + unit + basis + source + locator
Metrics in a semantic layer: the model picks, code computes
Few sharp tools, instructive errors, compact results
Loop: context → model → tools → observe → verify → answer

captions: Part six. Your build plan.
What to install, what to build first, and
how to know it works.
Here's the stack. Small, local, and boring on
purpose.
Python with U V.
The Claude API, with Sonnet five running the
loop and Haiku doing cheap extraction.
DuckDB as the single engine.
Docling to parse PDFs locally.
LanceDB plus keyword search for commentary.
And Mem0, the open source version, for long-term
memory.
And here's the repository.
Raw inputs go in the data folder. Seed
it with three companies you actually follow.
The harness folder holds the loop, the context
builder, and the tools.
The real value sits in three folders: ingest,
the semantic layer, and the verifier.
Traces go to a J S O N
L file. And the golden eval set sits
beside a simple command line.
Build it in this order.
Phase zero, setup.
Phase one, a minimal loop with one SQL
tool over an Excel file. You'll have something
working on day one.
Phase two, ingestion. PDFs become facts and chunks.
Phase three, the semantic layer.
Phase four, the verifier and citations.
Phase five, memory.
Phase six, evals and traces. That one never
really ends.
And phase seven, extend. Expose your tools over
M C P, so Claude Code can use
your harness too. Add sub-agents, and live prices.
So where do you start this week?
Day one: one loop, one tool, and one
Excel file. Ask it for revenue over four
quarters, and read the trace.
Then earn every new feature with an eval.
The full plan, with the research and every
source, is in the companion note.
Let's recap.
The model is the engine. The harness is
the car.
Prepare data before the question.
Keep one facts table, where every value carries
its provenance.
Put metrics in a semantic layer, so code
computes and the model only chooses.
Keep tools few and sharp.
Run a simple loop that verifies before it
answers.
Let memory store corrections, not numbers.
And measure everything.
The goal: every number traceable to a cell.
The example numbers were illustrative, and none of
this is investment advice. Thanks for watching.
